paper_title: The Lexical Imprint of Pre-training Data

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: How much of zero-shot benchmark accuracy is captured by word-level alignment between a pre-training corpus and the benchmark target? We study this question through word-level unigram cross-entropy (UCE), a tokenizer-agnostic, model-free measure of lexical alignment between a reference corpus and a target benchmark. Likelihood training shapes the model's predictive distribution from the pre-training corpus, and zero-shot scores under likelihood-based evaluation depend in part on the lexical alignment between that corpus and the benchmark target. Cleanly tracing how the lexical imprint of pre-training data scales with corpus--benchmark alignment requires controlled from-scratch pre-training that varies corpus identity while holding the training recipe fixed. Across this controlled sweep, spanning $10$ zero-shot benchmarks, $4$ pre-training corpora, and $3$ model scales, we find that corpus--benchmark lexical alignment, UCE, consistently tracks zero-shot accuracy on every benchmark, with corpora more aligned with the benchmark (lower UCE) achieving higher accuracy. The same signal extends from measurement to control at finer scopes. At the document level, strengthening the imprint by selecting training documents to maximize lexical alignment with the benchmark produces the accuracy gains predicted by the mechanism. At the prompt level, matching the imprint per prompt by routing each prompt to the drafter whose domain corpus is most lexically aligned with it produces measurable throughput gains over a generalist-drafter baseline. Taken together, pre-training corpora leave a measurable lexical imprint on base-model zero-shot behavior, and UCE provides a model-free probe of lexical alignment between reference and target data.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Modern language models are typically assessed on zero-shot benchmarks, which are constructed around representative problem formulations and treated as quantitative measurements of model capability [16]. quantitative account of how distinct the benchmark distribution is from the pre-training corpus is natural input to interpreting such accuracy. This relationship has been studied at the level of individual benchmark items and pieces of the lexicon, where term-level frequency of benchmark vocabulary tracks few-shot accuracy [7], test-instance lexical popularity correlates with task performance [8], and corpus-side perplexity signatures predict performance across panels of pretrained models [9]. These post-hoc analyses operate on pretrained checkpoints, and the corpus identity that drives the lexical signal is entangled with training recipe, scale, and training history. Figure 1: Training on corpus with word distribution leaves lexical imprint on the model, partly visible in likelihood scores on target benchmark with word distribution Q. Word-level unigram cross-entropy (UCE), tokenizer-agnostic measure of alignment, is proxy for this imprint. Across training corpora, lower UCE goes with higher zero-shot accuracy on the same benchmark. Selecting training documents that lower UCE strengthens the imprint and raises target accuracy. Routing each prompt to the drafter whose corpus has the lowest UCE against it raises decoding speed. alignment therefore calls for controlled from-scratch pre-training across corpora, setting in which this alignment remains under-characterized at scale. Empirical evidence suggests that models achieving lower training loss on high-quality pre-training data tend to attain stronger downstream performance [1012]. This relationship is consistent with the compression view of language modeling [1315], under which likelihood-based predictions on benchmark data are expected to be more reliable when training and benchmark distributions are close. Concretely, how much of zero-shot benchmark performance can the corpusbenchmark distributional alignment alone explain? We approach this question information-theoretically, by summarizing both the pre-training corpus and benchmark target through their word-level unigram distributions and treating their cross-entropy (UCE) as measure of distributional alignment. We adopt the word as the fundamental unit since words are discrete, semantically meaningful elements of language4. Across corpora, benchmark vocabulary is fully covered during pre-training, so zero-shot performance differences are driven by how probability mass is allocated over benchmark-relevant words. The lower unigram cross-entropy reflects closer alignment of corpus-benchmark word-distribution and predicts higher zero-shot accuracy in all benchmarks we test. This admits simple interpretation. Likelihood-based pre-training learns conditional distribution from the training corpus, while zero-shot evaluation performs probabilistic inference using the learned distribution by scoring the conditional likelihoods of benchmark candidates. Corpus-level word-distribution alignment may therefore provide low-order proxy connecting training data to benchmark behavior. Contributions. We propose unigram cross-entropy (UCE) as single corpus-side lens for tracing the lexical imprint of pre-training data on zero-shot behavior, applied at three points of the languagemodel lifecycle (Figure 1). (i) At the corpus level. Across the controlled from-scratch sweep, UCE matches the zero-shot accuracy ordering on every benchmark, with cross-corpus differences captured by how probability mass is allocated to benchmark-relevant words. (ii) At the document level. Treating UCE as per-document objective gives the unigram cross-entropy filter (UCE-filter), which controls document-level lexical alignment under fixed token budget. Under the same from-scratch grid, alignment-driven selection reproduces the corpus-level UCEaccuracy relationship at the document scope. (iii) At the prompt level. In speculative decoding with pool of corpus-specialized drafters, evaluating UCE between each prompt and each drafters training corpus produces third instance of the same functional acting at finer scope, with measurable throughput gains over generalist-drafter baseline. Together, through this exploration, lexical alignment between pre-training corpus and benchmark target, measured by word-level unigram cross-entropy, provides measurable trace of the lexical imprint that pre-training data leaves on zero-shot behavior. 4We follow the standard lexicographic notion of word as the smallest meaningful unit of speech that can stand by itself (cf. the Oxford English Dictionary entry for word).

sections.title: 2 Motivation: From Likelihood Training to Lexical Imprints
sections.content: The downstream performance of modern pre-trained language models is typically assessed by selecting the least surprising candidate under the learned distribution, that is, choosing the option with the highest conditional likelihood given the input [16]5. By maximizing next-token likelihood over the training corpus, language-model pre-training estimates empirical conditional patterns, producing parametric approximation to the data-generating distribution through empirical cross-entropy minimization [1318]. Accordingly, neural language models can be viewed as parametric conditional estimators analogous to classical n-gram models, as both aim to approximate the underlying conditional distribution despite differing parameterizations. This view motivates the working hypothesis that the models predicted conditional distribution is, at least approximately, aligned with that statistically estimated from its training data. This hypothesis is supported by empirical and theoretical findings showing that neural language models often capture low-order n-gram statistics, particularly in early training, and that such n-gram statistics provide meaningful and relatively tight lower bound on model expressivity [1921]. Moreover, higher-order n-gram models trained on sufficient data can improve the performance of language models when combined with them [22]. From this perspective, likelihood-based pre-training learns conditional distribution from the training corpus, while zero-shot evaluation performs probabilistic inference under that distribution by selecting the most likely candidate. Although this structure is infeasible to estimate directly at corpus scale, the corpus-level word-frequency distribution may provide tractable low-order proxy for the shared dependence between pre-training data and downstream behavior. We refer to this trace as the lexical imprint of pre-training data on zero-shot behavior, made measurable through corpusbenchmark word-distribution alignment. This leads to central research question. How much of zero-shot benchmark performance is captured by the alignment between corpus and benchmark word distributions? quantitative answer would distinguish accuracy gains attributable to corpus alignment from gains reflecting generalization beyond it. Direct estimation of conditional alignment at corpus scale is intractable, so Section 3 operationalizes this question through tractable word-distribution proxy that bridges the pre-training corpus and the benchmark target.

sections.title: 3 Measuring Lexical Alignment with Unigram Cross-Entropy
sections.content: Our goal is to empirically evaluate how alignment between the conditional distributions of the training and benchmark data affects language model performance. We first introduce word-level unigram cross-entropy (UCE) as stable and efficient proxy for measuring this alignment (Section 3.1), and then motivate the use of word-level unigram cross-entropy as the primary metric (Section 3.2). 3.1 Definition of Unigram Cross-Entropy Conditional distributions and entropy rates are difficult to estimate directly at corpus scale because of finite-sample bias, data sparsity, smoothing sensitivity, and the limited reliability of long-context statistics, so we proxy them with the word-level unigram distribution (Figure 1). The proxy is coarse but computationally efficient, robust to sparsity, and implicitly reflects character-level n-gram structure since individual words contain rich non-i.i.d. character patterns [23]. Let and denote the empirical word-frequency distributions of the pre-training corpus and the benchmark dataset, which we call the reference distribution and the target distribution, respectively. Up to the constant H(Q), UCE equals the KL divergence between and , so it provides clean measure of their overlap. Appendix collects further corpus-level analyses, including comparison against alternative lexical alignment measures (Appendix D.5), the pairwise separation of the corpora themselves (Appendix D.6), and capability families outside the statistics scope (Appendix D.7). 3.2 Why Words and Unigrams? We adopt word-level unigram cross-entropy for two reasons. First, subword tokenizers are manyto-one mappings, so token-level cross-entropy conflates genuine distributional mismatch with segmentation artefacts induced by token boundaries that do not align with the true data-generating process [24, 25]. Word-level granularity removes this confound by operating at unit common to the corpus and the benchmark. Second, although higher-order n-gram cross-entropy for fixed decomposes into target-dependent constant and conditional KL divergence between the two datasets, reliable estimation at corpus scale is hindered by sparsity in the context space, making the estimate sensitive to finite-sample bias and smoothing choices. Word-level unigram cross-entropy instead decomposes exactly into the marginal entropy of the target distribution and the KL divergence between the corresponding word distributions. It therefore avoids the estimation difficulties associated with higher-order conditional statistics. The unigram decomposition is provided in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4 Corpus-Level Lexical Alignment Tracks Zero-Shot Behavior
sections.content: This section examines whether the word-level unigram cross-entropy (UCE) of Section 3 tracks zero-shot benchmark accuracy at the corpus level, and whether the trend is stable across pre-training corpora, model scales, and random subsamples. 4.1 From-Scratch Pre-training and Evaluation Protocol For the training setup, we pre-train decoder-only Transformer models [26] from scratch at three scales (400M, 1.33B, 3.36B) on four pre-training corpora spanning range of data quality, namely the highquality FineWeb-Edu [27] and DCLM [28], the earlier high-quality C4 [29], and the comparatively lower-quality OpenWebText [30]. From C4, DCLM, and FineWeb-Edu we draw three random sub-samples of 8.5B, 26B, and 60B tokens. The matched (model, subset) pairings (400M, 8.5B), (1.33B, 26B), and (3.36B, 60B) each sit at or near the Chinchilla compute-optimal ratio of 20 tokens 4 per parameter [31]. OpenWebText is only 9B tokens in total and is therefore evaluated at the 8.5B scale only. All from-scratch runs in this section and in Section 5.2 use AdamW with warmup and cosine learning-rate decay, sequence length of 2048, and global batch size of 256, and count tokens with the GPT-2 tokenizer [32]. The two studies differ in peak learning rate, warmup length, β2, and weight decay (Appendix C, Tables 69). For the evaluation setup, we measure zero-shot performance on pool of 12 benchmarks (ARC Easy [33], ARC Challenge [33], HellaSwag [34], MMLU [3], SciQ [35], OpenBookQA [36], PIQA [37], LAMBADA [38], SocialIQA [39], SWAG [40], CommonsenseQA [41], and BoolQ [42]). This section uses the 10 benchmarks other than CommonsenseQA and BoolQ, and the UCE-filter study of Section 5.2 uses the 11 other than MMLU. Per-task metrics differ between the two studies and are listed in Appendix C.1. Each corpus is used as released, and Section 7.2 audits all four with 13-gram index over the 12 benchmarks and tests whether removing the overlapping benchmark items or training documents changes the UCE-filter results. 4.2 Lexical Alignment Matches Corpus-Level Benchmark Rankings To assess whether corpusbenchmark alignment in word-frequency distributions predicts downstream performance and ranks pre-training corpora accordingly, we measure the UCE between every training subset of Section 4.1 and each of the 10 benchmarks, and compare the corpus ranking by UCE with the ranking by downstream score at each (model, subset) pairing. For 3.36B model trained on 60B tokens, Figure 2 shows that UCE predicts the accuracy order of the three corpora on all eight benchmarks. The newer DCLM and FineWeb-Edu, commonly regarded as higher-quality data [27, 28], lead with the lowest UCE on six of them, FineWeb-Edu on the knowledge-heavy ARC Easy/Challenge, SciQ, and OpenBookQA, and DCLM on SocialIQA and SWAG. Their UCE is higher than C4s wherever they trail C4, on HellaSwag and PIQA for both and on SocialIQA and SWAG for FineWeb-Edu. UCE thus tracks the task-dependent overlap that quality reputation misses, and this overlap plays central role in shaping downstream performance. Because curation and genre also vary across these corpora, the corpus-level UCEaccuracy relationship is associational, and Section 5 tests it within each source corpus at fixed token budget. Decomposing the corpusbenchmark overlap shows that all four corpora attain near-saturated coverage of the benchmark vocabulary at our scales and differ in how they allocate probability mass over that vocabulary. On every benchmark in Figure 2, the higher corpus scores, the smaller the share of benchmark word mass that falls on its long tail of rare words. Appendix D.1 discusses this decomposition, and Appendix D.4 shows that the inverse relationship between performance and UCE holds across the 10 benchmarks, dataset sizes, and model scales. 4.3 The Imprint Is Stable Across Random Subsets To test whether the inverse relationship depends on the specific subset chosen, we draw five different 8.5B-token subsets each from C4, DCLM, and FineWeb-Edu and one from OpenWebText, then pre-train 400M model on each. The inverse relationship holds across the 16 runs in Figure 3 (R2 = 0.928 on ARC Easy and 0.805 on PIQA). Within each corpus the subsets have nearly the same UCE and differ little in accuracy. The fluctuations are consistent with run-to-run noise rather than systematic sensitivity to subset composition. Appendix D.4 gives the per-task results for each subset.

sections.title: 7 Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: 7.1 One Alignment Functional Across Corpora, Documents, and Prompts Maximizing next-token likelihood minimizes KL divergence to the empirical training distribution. To first order, this aligns the models word predictions on Vb with the corpus word distribution, while higher-order conditional structure is learned later and only partially, especially on the long tail [19, 21, 55]. The descriptive result of Section 4.2 is therefore structural consequence of this ordering and reflects the optimization geometry shared by likelihood training and likelihood scoring rather than properties specific to the scales or corpora we examine. These results suggest that likelihood-based zero-shot performance partly reflects corpusbenchmark lexical alignment, alongside the capabilities each benchmark is intended to assess. The three uses of UCE in this paper are three instantiations of the same DKL(Q ) functional at different scopes. Corpus-level ranking (Section 4) evaluates DKL once per (corpus, benchmark) pair to compare web-scale training corpora. Row-local data selection (Section 5) evaluates the marginal contribution of each row to DKL and removes the rows whose removal most lowers it. Per-prompt drafter routing (Section 6) evaluates DKL between each prompts word distribution and each drafters corpus word distribution, and assigns the prompt to the drafter with the lowest DKL. 7.2 Contamination as an Alternative Explanation Benchmark text inside pre-training corpus could raise lexical alignment and accuracy together. We audit samples of all four corpora with GPT-3-style word-level 13-gram index [56]  (Table 5)  . Nine of the 12 benchmarks have under 0.3% of items matched in every sample, and the three exceptions, BoolQ, SciQ, and MMLU, peak on FineWeb-Edu. On SWAG, SocialIQA, and LAMBADA, where at most 0.01% of items match on C4, DCLM, or FineWeb-Edu, corpus with lower UCE still scores better, so contamination is unlikely to explain the relationship there. Among the three exceptions, BoolQ supplies its passage at evaluation time, so match on that passage cannot carry the yes or no label. The audit does not rule out contribution on SciQ and MMLU, where FineWeb-Edu has both the most matched items and the highest score. In the selection study, the UCE-filters gain over the random control survives contamination removal at both ends (Appendix F). The training-end removal drops 0.13% of DCLM rows, re-scan of one-million-document samples of each re-selected subset finds no remaining match, and each subsets UCE moves by at most 0.005 bits. Benchmark memorization alone is therefore unlikely to explain the gain, although the retraining check covers only DCLM at 1.34B. 7.3 What Unigram Cross-Entropy Captures and Where It Fails UCE measures only the alignment of word distributions. It is by construction blind to conditional structure such as syntax, multi-token composition, and factual co-occurrence, so UCE is best understood as lower-bound proxy for distributional alignment rather than sufficient summary of corpus quality or fundamental property of the models. UCE does not order grammar (BLiMP [57]), arithmetic (MathQA [58]), or non-English (Global-PIQA [59]) benchmarks (Appendix D.7). Whitespace tokenization is second boundary, since UCE applies most directly to whitespace-segmented languages and leaves non-segmented scripts (e.g., Chinese, Japanese) and highly agglutinative morphologies for future work. Apart from the routing study, the 30B case study, and 5-shot checks, every claim concerns basemodel zero-shot behavior under controlled from-scratch protocol, and the selection gains are an upper bound under known target (Section 5.2). Two directions follow directly from our design, paraphrase protocol that tests how far the observed relationship depends on exact lexical realization, and lexical decomposition that restricts UCE to benchmark-characteristic vocabulary. Whether the lexical imprint persists through SFT and RLHF, which differ from pre-training in data volume, training objective, and what is measured, requires controlled study built for those objectives. general account of what makes model generalize would need design that varies the other properties of pre-training data along with this lexical one.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Pre-trained language-model behavior is shaped by many intertwined factors, including higher-order conditional structure, scale, and post-training reshaping. This paper takes up one of them, the lexical imprint that the pre-training corpus leaves on zero-shot behavior, as captured by word-level unigram cross-entropy. Its descriptive force comes from single mechanism. Likelihood training allocates probability mass according to the pre-training corpus, and likelihood-based zero-shot evaluation partly reflects the lexical alignment between the pre-training corpus and the benchmark target. This descriptive signal becomes the same statistic at finer scopes. Applied as document-level data selection, it controls the lexical imprint, and this control shows it more clearly than comparing corpora can, since accuracy rises mainly on the target whose alignment is raised. Applied as prompt-level drafter routing, it raises speculative-decoding throughput. Across these uses, the analytic relationship between pre-training corpus, benchmark target, and language-model behavior is measured rather than only described. The same logic marks the limits of the account. UCE ignores syntax, multi-token composition and the effects of post-training. It makes one part of the imprint measurable, namely how the lexical statistics of pre-training data align with those of the target data. We close with: Pre-training pulls models predictive distribution toward its corpuss empirical conditional patterns, leaving measurable lexical imprint on zero-shot behavior.

sections.title: B Related Work
sections.content: Lexical traces of pre-training data. line of work has linked lexical signals to language-model behavior at increasingly coarse granularities. Razeghi et al. [7] link item-level term frequency to few-shot numerical reasoning, Kandpal et al. [55] extend this to entity-level long-tail frequency in QA, Wang et al. [60] formalize distributional memorization between LLM output probabilities and per-task n-gram counts, and Ruzzetti et al. [8] relate test-instance lexical popularity to performance. Closest in spirit, Wu et al. [9] mine salient tokens from in-the-wild web corpora whose token-level perplexity, taken over panel of 32 pretrained models, predicts performance on 89 benchmarks. Across all of these, the lexical signal is measured on pretrained checkpoints, and the corpus identity that drives it is entangled with training recipe, scale, tokenizer, and training history. We instead vary corpus identity under fixed from-scratch recipe (Section 4.1) and intervene on document-level alignment (Section 5). Compression and Markov approximations. Section 2 discusses work that frames language modeling as compression of the training distribution [13, 15] and likelihood training as estimation of the empirical data distribution [17], together with work relating neural language models to n-gram statistics [1921]. Data selection. Aligning training data with downstream target has long history. Klakow [61] trains unigram language model on the full non-domain corpus and scores each candidate segment by how removing it would change the in-domain data log-likelihood under that model. Moore and Lewis [44] introduce the cross-entropy difference filter, while Axelrod [62] and Feng et al. [63] develop cynical data selection, greedy method that chooses sentences by how much adding each one improves the language-model likelihood of the target-domain data. More recently, Xie et al. [43] scale importance resampling using hashed n-gram features, and Thrush et al. [64] use the correlation of per-domain LLM perplexity with downstream accuracy across 90 LMs as selection signal. Magnusson et al. [65] use small-scale proxy models to predict which pre-training data yields the best models at larger scale across downstream benchmarks. The UCE-filter shares this goal but operationalizes alignment as single information-theoretic functional requiring only word counts, with the same statistic that drives our descriptive analysis (Section 4.2) reused as the row-local selection signal (Section 5.1). Appendix E.3 compares the UCE-filter with the embedding-based selector BETR [45] under our from-scratch grid. Benchmark contamination. Another line of work treats the corpusevaluation interface as contamination problem at the level of exact or near-exact overlap [66], supported by large-scale corpus auditing [67]. UCE complements contamination detection by summarizing the interface at the coarser level of probability mass on benchmark words rather than exact-match overlap. Appendix reports our own 13-gram audit of the four corpora, with contaminated items and documents removed at the evaluation and training ends. Speculative decoding. Section 6 routes between corpus-specialized drafters using unigram crossentropy. The base setup follows Leviathan et al. [47] and Chen et al. [48]. Among learned routing policies, Hou et al. [68] use bandit-based drafter selection and Wu et al. [69] adapt across multiple drafter levels, while Hong et al. [70] report best practices for training domain-specialized drafters. separate model-free direction retrieves candidates from non-parametric text statistics [71, 72]. UCErouting keeps the parametric drafter pool fixed and selects among them via precomputed corpus-level unigram distribution, with no per-prompt training, online learning, or retrieval at inference.

sections.title: F Contamination audit and removal
sections.content: Contamination could inflate both lexical alignment and benchmark accuracy at once, so we audit it independently rather than relying on the corpus curators procedures, and then remove it at both the evaluation end and the training end. Protocol. The audit follows the word-level 13-gram protocol of GPT-3 [56], with the scan repeated under the protocol variants of Brown et al. [56], Messmer et al. [73], Chowdhery et al. [74] and the 80% near-duplicate criterion of Llama 2 [26]. The n-grams are built with the filters own normalizer (NFKC, punctuation stripped, whitespace split, case preserved), so the audit measures the same text the metric measures. Each item enters as its full evaluation text (passage, question, and every option, with no answer field), the same text that defines the target distribution Q. The index covers 12 benchmarks and 303,139 items, and the item-share scan covers spread samples of up to one million documents from each of the four corpora. Nine of the twelve tasks match under 0.3% of items in every sample  (Table 5)  . The three exceptions (BoolQ, SciQ, MMLU) peak on FineWeb-Edu, whose educational filtering overlaps encyclopedic passages, and the matches are passage-side surface overlap rather than answer leakage. Removal at the evaluation end. We flag every scored evaluation item sharing 13-gram with the corpus and re-score without them, comparing each arm at one matched training seed (three-seed means are in Table 2). On DCLM this removes 161 of 36,934 CSR7 items (HellaSwag 80, SciQ 65, ARC-Easy 8, PIQA 6, ARC-Challenge 2), and the UCE-filter advantage over the random control moves from 3.11 to 3.16 pp at 3.33B and from 4.13 to 4.16 pp at 1.34B. On FineWeb-Edu the removal covers 163 items (SciQ 106, HellaSwag 45, ARC-Easy 6, ARC-Challenge 4, PIQA 2), and the advantage moves from 2.05 to 2.10 pp at 3.33B and from 2.86 to 2.88 pp at 1.34B. The advantage is therefore unchanged in all four cells. Removal at the training end. On the full DCLM source of 630M rows we remove every row sharing 13-gram with the index (0.13% of rows), re-run each selection rule over the surviving rows at the same 20% budget (126M rows), and retrain 1.34B from scratch on 70B tokens under the papers recipe, comparing each arm against its own training seed. Re-scanning one-million-document samples of each new subset finds zero remaining matches. The CSR7 accuracy of all three arms moves within run-to-run noise  (Table 31)  . Each arms subset UCE shifts by at most 0.005 bits under the same measurement pass, so the selection signal itself is untouched. The UCE-filter keeps +3.40 pp over the random control against +4.13 pp before, with the ordering unchanged. sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract states UCE as model-free, tokenizer-agnostic measure of corpus benchmark word-distribution alignment, the descriptive finding that lower UCE tracks higher zero-shot accuracy on every benchmark, and the two prescriptive interventions (documentlevel data selection and prompt-level drafter routing). The Introductions Contributions paragraph restates these as three observations (corpus, document, prompt) under one alignment functional, with the scope qualifier that UCE-filter is controlled probe rather than stand-alone data-selection method. The claims match the experimental scope and the limits in Section 7. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 7 discusses (i) what UCE does not capture (conditional structure such as syntax, and the grammar, arithmetic, and non-English benchmarks of Appendix D.7), (ii) the whitespace-tokenization caveat for non-segmented or agglutinative scripts, and (iii) the target-adapted nature of the UCE-filter when is estimated from the evaluation tasks. Section 5.3 adds the 30B case-study caveats. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. 41 While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix states the assumptions (stationarity of PA and PB, well-defined entropy rates) and gives the unigram identity H(pB, pA) = H(pB) + DKL(pBpA). Maintext Section 3 cross-references the appendix at the equation level. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix report the training recipe (optimizer AdamW, cosine LR schedule with warmup, batch size, sequence length, and weight decay) and the per-scale architecture for both the corpus-ranking grid (LLaMA pattern, Tables 67) and the UCE-filter grid (DataComp-LM pattern, Tables 89), with gradient clipping and BF16 precision also listed for the UCE-filter grid. The UCE-filter algorithm is given in Algorithm 1, and the code at https://github.com/penpaperkeycode/lexical-imprint provides reference implementations of UCE, the UCE-filter, the DSIR baseline, and the benchmark preprocessing pipeline. All pre-training corpora and benchmarks are public. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The code is released at https://github.com/penpaperkeycode/ lexical-imprint. It covers the word-level UCE metric (unigram_ce/), the UCE-filter with multi-worker analytic-H row scoring (ce_filter/), the DSIR baseline with hashedbigram importance resampling and optional Gumbel top-K (dsir/), benchmark preprocessing for the evaluation tasks of Sections 4.1 and 5.2 (benchmarks/), and tiny endto-end demo (dsir/examples/tiny_demo/). Each subdirectory has its own quick-start README.md. The from-scratch pre-training runs follow the recipes in Appendix C, with the LLaMA pattern for the corpus-ranking grid and the DataComp-LM pattern for the UCE-filter grid. All pre-training corpora (C4, DCLM, FineWeb-Edu, OpenWebText) and benchmarks are publicly available, with evaluation through lm-evaluation-harness [16]. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] 43 Justification: Section 4.1 states the shared pre-training protocol and the corpus-ranking setup (corpora, sub-sample sizes, model scales, benchmark pool). Section 5.2 states the UCE-filter setup (sources, scales, top-20% retention, baselines, target suite). Section 6 states the routing setup (verifier, three OpenThoughts-114k [50] specialist drafters under the SAM architecture [51], generalist-drafter baseline, and AIME/LiveCodeBench/MMLU/MedQA evaluation). The pre-training hyperparameters of the corpus-ranking and UCE-filter grids are in Appendix C. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Within-corpus stability (Figure 3, Section 4.3) reports per-corpus mean 1σ across 16 random 8.5B-token subsets at 400M scale, with an OLS fit, 95% CI band, R2, Spearman ρ, and p-value. Table 2 reports mean std across 3 training seeds (1234, 42, 7777) per (Source, Scale, Selection) cell for UCE-filter, Random, and DSIR-paper, totaling 36 from-scratch runs across the 223 grid (Appendix E.8). UCE values in Table 1 are selection-deterministic for UCE-Filter and Full, while Random and DSIR vary by less than 0.001 bits across 3 data-selection seeds. per-task accuracy breakdown is in Table 32. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All from-scratch runs use NVIDIA B200 GPUs (183GB HBM, 8 per node) on shared cluster. Selection. UCE and the UCE-filter run on single CPU-only pod (120 cores, no GPU). At the 70B-token output budget the UCE-filter end-to-end wall-time is 44 roughly 3.58.3h per source on 120-core pod, with aggregate CPU-hours comparable to DSIRs. Training. Each cell of the UCE-filter grid (Section 5.2) uses 16 B200 GPUs across two nodes for 70B GPT-2 tokens, with per-cell wall-time of approximately 7h at 1.34B and 17h at 3.33B. The grid covers four selection methods, two sources, and two scales, with UCE-filter, Random, and DSIR-paper at 3 seeds and DSIR-LN at 1 seed (40 runs total). The corpus-ranking grid (Section 4.1) is of the same order. The 30B Stage-2 case study (Section 5.3) runs on in-house infrastructure (2T-token baseline vs 200Btoken UCE-filtered variant). Inference-time experiments (Section 6) are single-node and negligible. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The work uses only publicly available corpora and benchmarks, conducts no human-subject research, releases no new personal data, and follows the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Positive. UCE-filter reduces compute spent on uninformative pre-training data, and routing reduces inference cost at fixed model quality. Alignment diagnostics make corpusbenchmark proximity legible, supporting transparent benchmarking. Negative. Target-aware curation can hack benchmark scores in ways that overstate underlying capability, and over-reliance on benchmark-aligned data may degrade out-of-distribution generalization. Reporting UCE next to accuracy is partial mitigation, since Section 7.1 notes that zero-shot accuracy partly reflects lexical alignment, and Section 5.2 reports out-of-target accuracy beside the targeted suite. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. 45 The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper releases no model or dataset that poses high misuse risk. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Every dataset and code package is cited at first reference. Pre-training corpora (C4 [29], DCLM [28], FineWeb-Edu [27], OpenWebText [30]) and evaluation benchmarks (ARC [33], HellaSwag [34], MMLU [3], MMLU-Pro [4], SciQ [35], OpenBookQA [36], PIQA [37], LAMBADA [38], BoolQ [42], Social IQa [39], CommonsenseQA [41], SWAG [40]) are used under their published licenses. Routing experiments (Section 6) use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B [49] as the verifier and AIME [52], LiveCodeBench [53], and MedQA [54] as benchmarks, with specialist drafters trained on OpenThoughts-114k [50] under the SAM architecture [51]. The verifier is released under the MIT License, and its model card states that it is derived from Llama-3.1-8B, which is distributed under the Llama 3.1 Community License. Evaluation runs through lm-evaluation-harness [16]. Tokenization uses GPT-2 [32] byte-level BPE. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. 46 For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We release reference implementation of the UCE-filter (Algorithm 1) including row-scoring and multi-worker batched scoring at https://github.com/ penpaperkeycode/lexical-imprint. The 1.34B and 3.33B from-scratch base-model checkpoints from Section 5.2 will be uploaded to HuggingFace upon request. Both are accompanied by README/model cards listing training data, hyperparameters (Appendix C), intended research use, and known limitations. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper involves no crowdsourcing or human-subject research. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: No human-subject research, so IRB review is not applicable. 47 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [N/A] Justification: The core methodology (UCE, the UCE-filter, UCE-based drafter routing) does not use LLMs as research instrument. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
